intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP8A2 gene (605870) on chromosome 13q12.

checks.claim: Cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP8A2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Altogether, 6 of the 7 homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations known in ATP8A2 located in this subregion (amino acids 364‐877) of the catalytic cytoplasmic domain.
checks.explanation: Paper reports homozygous and compound heterozygous ATP8A2 mutations causing CAMRQ4.

checks.claim: The ATP8A2 gene is located on chromosome 13q12.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity mapping revealed that several shared homozygous regions, including chromosome 13q12.
checks.explanation: The abstract names 13q12 as a homozygous region and then identifies the ATP8A2 variant, which implies ATP8A2 lies there. It never states the gene's location directly.

paragraphs.text: Cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability, and cerebellar atrophy, with quadrupedal locomotion in some affected individuals (Onat et al., 2013; Mohamadian et al., 2020). Other reported features include severe hypotonia, dysarthria, areflexia, and, in some patients, athetosis, ophthalmoplegia, and visual and hearing impairment (Mohamadian et al., 2020; Narishige et al., 2022). The phenotypic spectrum also includes a less severe form of congenital ataxia with near-normal cognition (Damasio et al., 2021).

checks.claim: CAMRQ4 is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: The pattern of inheritance in all of the possible phenotypes is autosomal recessive.
checks.explanation: Also abstract: 'rare and early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder'.

checks.claim: CAMRQ4 is characterized by cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability, and cerebellar atrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: Missense mutation in the ATPase, aminophospholipid transporter protein ATP8A2 is associated with cerebellar atrophy and quadrupedal locomotion.
checks.explanation: The title names cerebellar atrophy, and the condition studied is cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation and dysequilibrium syndrome.

checks.claim: Some individuals with CAMRQ4 show quadrupedal locomotion.
checks.evidence_quote: Missense mutation in the ATPase, aminophospholipid transporter protein ATP8A2 is associated with cerebellar atrophy and quadrupedal locomotion.
checks.explanation: The title links the mutation to quadrupedal locomotion.

checks.claim: Reported features of CAMRQ4 include severe hypotonia, dysarthria, and areflexia.
checks.evidence_quote: The other possible clinical features are severe hypotonia, retarded motor development, dysarthria, seizures, optic atrophy, and short stature.
checks.explanation: Areflexia is supported by 'In these patients, deep tendon reflexes were absent.'

checks.claim: Some patients with CAMRQ4 have athetosis, ophthalmoplegia, and visual and hearing impairment.
checks.evidence_quote: visual and hearing impairments associated with involuntary movements and severe developmental delay may be a clue to suspect CAMRQ4
checks.explanation: Athetotic movements, ophthalmoplegia, retinal degeneration/optic atrophy and flattened ABRs are reported.

checks.claim: The phenotypic spectrum of CAMRQ4 includes a less severe form of congenital ataxia with near-normal cognition.
checks.evidence_quote: These results allowed us to establish this as a disease-causing variant and expand ATP8A2-related disorders to include less severe forms of congenital ataxia.
checks.explanation: The abstract states the spectrum expansion, and the patients had near-normal cognition.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) described 3 sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family of Arab descent born to healthy first-cousin parents: a 9-year-old girl (the proband), her 15-year-old sister, and her 17-year-old brother. They had non-progressive cerebellar ataxia, severe hypotonia, intellectual disability, dysarthria, and cerebellar atrophy. The proband had severe neonatal hypotonia, global psychomotor delay, and feeding difficulties since infancy. She used a wheelchair and was unable to walk, sit, or hold her head. All 3 patients had an IQ of 20 to 40, delayed speech with dysarthria, absent deep tendon reflexes, and cerebellar atrophy on brain MRI. Hearing was normal, there were no seizures or optic atrophy, and metabolic investigations were normal.

paragraphs.text: Narishige et al. (2022) reported 2 Japanese sibs with CAMRQ4 who presented with athetotic movements at 1 and 2 months of age. They also had ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, feeding difficulty, hypotonia, and severely delayed development. One sib had retinal degeneration and optic atrophy. Flattening of auditory brainstem responses and areflexia developed later. At last follow-up, neither patient could sit or achieve head control, although some nonverbal communication was preserved.

paragraphs.text: Ozcelik et al. (2008) studied 4 large consanguineous Turkish kindreds with quadrupedal gait (Unertan syndrome), which they described as a rare phenotype associated with dysarthric speech, mental retardation, and varying degrees of cerebrocerebellar hypoplasia. VLDLR mutations had been found in families A and D. In families B and C, the phenotype was not linked to chromosome 9p. The authors concluded that hereditary disorders with quadrupedal gait in humans are genetically heterogeneous. In a reply to Herz et al. (2008) and Humphrey et al. (2008), Ozcelik et al. (2008) further discussed the genetic heterogeneity of cerebellar hypoplasia with quadrupedal locomotion.

paragraphs.text: Gulsuner et al. (2011) studied a large consanguineous Turkish family with quadrupedal locomotion, mental retardation, and cerebro-cerebellar hypoplasia. Imaging showed abnormalities of the cerebellum and corpus callosum, including atrophy of the superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles. Additional morphometric abnormalities were seen in cortical areas, including the precentral gyrus and Brodmann areas BA6, BA44, and BA45. By homozygosity mapping, the authors linked the disorder to a 7.1-Mb region on chromosome 17p13.1-p13.3. Targeted sequencing of this region identified a homozygous P856L missense mutation in the WDR81 gene (614218) that cosegregated with the disorder. WDR81 is highly expressed in the cerebellum, particularly in the Purkinje cell layer. Gulsuner et al. (2011) noted that WDR81 was the third gene, after VLDLR and CA8, implicated in quadrupedal locomotion in humans.

paragraphs.text: In 3 affected sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family with CAMRQ4, Mohamadian et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition (NM_016529.6) in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene. The mutation results in a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution at an extremely conserved residue in the ATP-binding (N) domain. Karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis were normal, and the mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. It segregated with the disease: the parents and 2 unaffected sibs were heterozygous, and 1 unaffected sib was wildtype. The mutation was absent from public databases and from 100 ethnically matched controls. Structural modeling predicted reduced protein stability and an altered ligand-binding pocket.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with congenital ataxia, Damasio et al. (2021) used exome sequencing to identify a novel homozygous mutation in intron 17 of the ATP8A2 gene (c.1580-18C-G). Bioinformatics tools predicted that the mutation creates a new acceptor splice site. In a minigene assay in HEK293T cells, the mutant construct used an alternative acceptor splice site and produced an aberrant transcript that retained 17 bp of intron 17. This resulted in the insertion of 4 amino acids and a premature stop codon. The authors concluded that the variant was disease-causing.
